S Supporting Information ABSTRACT: Lignin dissolution is of great importance for the valorization of lignin, and development of novel efficient solvent systems is a crucial topic. Herein, 17 kinds of 1,5-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]-5-undecene-based eutectic molecular liquids (EMLs) were designed for dissolution of industrial lignins. The solubility of lignin in the EMLs significantly depended on the types of the EMLs and lignin. ## INTRODUCTION As the only renewable natural aromatic biopolymer, lignin could be utilized to produce various aromatic chemicals and functional materials, 1-5 which has received continuously increasing attention. Generally, an adequate solvent is necessary in most of the processes for lignin utilization. However, lignin was difficult to be dissolved in most common solvents owing to its complicated cross-linked three-dimensional structure. 6,7 Therefore, development of functional solvents to dissolve lignin is of great significance for lignin utilization, and much effort has been devoted on this important topic.

To date, several solvent systems have been developed for lignin dissolution, but some specific drawbacks existed in the corresponding systems. For example, the mixture of water and some organic solvents (e.g., polysorbate, 8 y-valerolactone, 9,10 and ethanol11,12) could be employed to dissolve lignin, but the high volatility of organic solvents was the main drawback of these systems. As the alternatives of organic solvent-based systems, ionic liquid (IL)-based systems have been successfully applied in lignin dissolution. 13-17 In spite of the good solubility of lignin, IL-based systems were limited by the high cost, not so good stability, and the use of toxic reagents and/or organic solvents in their synthetic routes. 18,19 Additionally, liquid ammonia had the ability to dissolve lignin, 20 but high pressure and too low temperature hampered its large-scale application. In another aspect, it is well-known that the resources and preparation methods significantly affected the structures and properties of lignin 21-23 and thus influenced the solubility of different lignin in one specific solvent. Based on the above discussion, it is a highly attractive issue to design
functional solvents with the purpose of efficiently and applicably dissolving different types of lignin.

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted tremendous attention as a class of green functional solvents applied in diverse areas. 24-28 Recently, several DESs has been successfully used in the dissolution of lignin. 29-31 However, the current developed DESs were generally based on quaternary ammonium salts, and their high viscosity limited their large- scale and practical applications for lignin dissolution due to the mass transfer between lignin and DESs. 32,33

Recently, eutectic molecular liquids (EMLs), an emerging type of solvents, have been proposed. 34,35 EMLs can be generated from two or more molecular compounds via various noncovalent interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonding, σ-hole bonding, π-hole bonding, κ-hole bonding, and μ-hole bonding).34 Compared with ionic DESs, EMLs could be formed from low-cost materials with lower viscosity. Meanwhile, the components in EMLs could be easily recovered and regenerated by evaporation, a significant merit over the general ionic DESs.36 Additionally, similar with ionic DESs, the properties of EMLs could be easily tuned by changing the components. These advantages make EMLs an attractive type of solvents for lignin dissolution, and novel solvents based on EMLs could be potentially designed to dissolve lignin efficiently.

By carefully pairing DBU with a suitable HBD and modifying the molar ratio of DBU/ HBD, these DBU-based EMLs could efficiently dissolve different types of lignin, including enzymatic hydrolysis lignin (EHL), organosolv lignin (OL), dealkaline lignin (DAL), and sodium lignosulfonate (SL).

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION **Synthesis of DBU-Based EMLs.** The DBU-based EMLs were initially synthesized by heating the mixture of DBU and the desired HBD (Scheme 1) with a suitable molar ratio. The detailed synthetic routes were provided in the Experimental Section. Meanwhile, the formed temperature for a specific EML and the suitable molar ratio of DBU/HBD capable of forming EMLs were provided in Table S1. It was revealed that a higher molar ratio of DBU/HBD was beneficial for the formation of EMLs at a lower heating temperature. For example, EMLs could be formed between DBU and all of the six HBDs with a DBU/HBD molar ratio of 2:1, and only PCA could not form EML with DBU at a DBU/HBD molar ratio of 1:1. However, when the DBU/HBD molar ratio was changed into 1:2 or 1:3, only three used HBDs (i.e., CPL, LA, and PEG) could generate EMLs with DBU. In addition, for practical applications, the physicochemical properties (i.e., viscosity and density) of the achieved EMLs were determined and provided in Tables S2 and S3.

Dissolution Behavior of Lignin in the DBU-Based EMLs. Dealkaline lignin (DAL) was selected as a model substrate to evaluate the ability of the synthesized EMLs for lignin dissolution. It was observed that almost all the prepared EMLs provided good solubility except for DBU-PEG-2:1 (Figure 1 and Table S4), and the solubility of DAL increased with the rising of temperature (from 30 to 90 °C) for all the formed EMLs because the viscosity of the EMLs decreased with the increased temperature (Table S2), 39,40 which was beneficial for DAL dissolution. When the DBU/HBD molar ratio became 1:1 (Figure 2b), DBU-PEG-1:1 was the best EML with a 38.8 wt% solubility at 90 °C (Table 1, entry 7). However, when the DBU/HBD molar ratio continually decreased to 1:2 and 1:3, only the EMLs formed with LA and PEG could dissolve EHL. Meanwhile, DBU-PEG-x showed better performance than DBU-LA-x at the same DBU/HBD

In another point of view, for the EMLs with the same HBD, the influence of the DBU/HBD molar ratio on EHL solubility varied significantly with the HBD types, and the orders were as follows: DBU-LA-1:3 > DBU-LA-2:1 > DBU-LA-1:2 > DBU-LA-1:1, DBU-BZA-2:1 > DBU-BZA-1:1, DBU-NMTU-2:1 > DBU-NMTU-1:1, and DBU-PEG-1:3 > DBU-PEG-1:2 ≈ DBU-PEG-1:1 > DBU-PEG-2:1. Second, as shown in Table S6, OL was difficult to be dissolved in most of the synthesized EMLs, and only DBU-LA-x could dissolve OL in all the used temperatures in most cases. The solubility of OL in DBU-LA-x followed the order: DBU-LA-1:3 > DBU-LA-1:2 > DBU-LA-2:1 > DBU-LA-1:1, and the highest solubility of 37.3 wt% was achieved in DBU-LA-1:3 at 90 °C (Table 1, entry 10). In addition, several EMLs could provide the satisfactory solubility of OL at a higher temperature (90 °C), including DBU-NMTU-2:1 (19.7 wt%), DBU-BZA-2:1 (12.7 wt%), DBU-PCA-2:1 (30.6 wt%), DBU-NMTU-1:1 (18.7 wt%), DBU-BZA-1:1 (22.1 wt%), DBU-PEG-1:2 (23.8 wt%), and DBU-PEG-1:3 (11.4 wt%). Third, it was found that only DBU-LA-x could dissolve SL (Table S7), which may be resulted from its salt-like structure. Meanwhile, the solubility of SL in DBU-LA-x increased with the decreasing DBU/LA molar ratio (Figure 2d), and DBU-LA-1:3 provided the highest solubility (38.3 wt%) at 90 °C (Table 1, entry 11). For comparison, the solubility of lignin from other literatures was listed in Table S8. It can be seen that the reported solvents either have poor solubility for lignin (e.g., the solubility of alkali lignin in malic acid/proline (1:3) is limited to 14.9 wt% even at 100 °C) or are expensive and environmentally non-benign (e.g., [P4441]-[MeSO4], [BMPyr][N(CN)2]).

On the basis of the above experiments, we could find that the solubility of lignin significantly depended on the types of the DBU-based EMLs (type of HBDs and DBU/HBD molar ratio) and lignin. It was observed that DBU-LA-x could dissolve all the four types of lignin at all examined temperatures except that DBU-LA-1:1 only showed good performance for OL dissolution at high temperatures (70 and 90 °C), indicating DBU-LA-x was the most adaptable EML to fit different types of lignin. Meanwhile, DAL could be dissolved by all the obtained EMLs except for DBU-PEG-2:1, while the types of EMLs, which could dissolve EHL, were less than those for DAL. Furthermore, OL was more difficult to be dissolved, and only DBU-LA-x could dissolve OL at all examined temperatures in most cases, while a high temperature (90 °C) was necessary for several other EMLs to dissolve OL (Table S6). Additionally, only DBU-LA-x could dissolve SL, and all other EMLs showed very poor solubility for SL even at 90 °C. These results implied that DAL was the most easily dissolved lignin because of the serious destruction of β-O-4 linkage in the preparation process, which was helpful for DAL dissolution, and the difficulty to dissolve SL was resulted from its salt-like structure.

Furthermore, a Kamlet–Taft linear solvation energy relationship (LSER) for quantifying solvent effects, which were introduced to investigate the correlations between the solubility and the Kamlet–Taft parameters of correspond- ing EMLs, were carried out, and the results are presented in Table 2.44,45
Table 2 shows that in most cases, the solubility of lignin is shown to be related to the hydrogen-bond donor property (a) and the Kamlet–Taft π* parameter of corresponding EMLs.

First, from Figure 1d, the four DBU-LA-_x_ could dissolve DAL efficiently with a solubility order of DBU-LA-1:3 > DBU-LA-1:2 ≈ DBU-LA-2:1 > DBU-LA-1:1. Table 2 and Figure 3b shows that there are positive correlations between the DAL solubilities and the Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters α and π*, but the correlation with β is not good. However, if the DBU-LA-2:1 is excluded, the positive correlations (DAL solubility with α and π*) and a negative correlation (DAL solubility with β) could be observed (Figure S1). The correlation between DAL solubility at 70 °C with the Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters follows the equation ln S = 1.09 + 4.11π* (Table 2). Also, DBU-LA-1:3 was the best EML in the DBU-LA-_x_ due to its highest polarity (π*) ability. Meanwhile, the three DBU-PEG-_x_ could dissolve DAL with a dissolution capability of DBU-PEG-1:3 > DBU-PEG-1:1 > DBU-PEG-1:2 (DBU-PEG-2:1 was not considered because DAL is almost insoluble in DBU-PEG-2:1). Table S9 shows that the values of α, β, and π* changed as the following orders: DBU-PEG-1:3 > DBU-PEG-1:2 > DBU-PEG-1:1 for π*, DBU-PEG-1:3 > DBU-PEG-1:1 > DBU-PEG-1:2 for α, and DBU-PEG-1:3 > DBU-PEG-1:1 > DBU-PEG-1:2 for β. The correlation between DAL solubility at 70 °C with the Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters obeys the equation: ln S = -2.49 + 8.29α (Table 2 and Figure 3c). DBU-PEG-1:3 showed the highest solubility for DAL owing to its strongest hydrogen-bond donating ability (the highest value of α) to form hydrogen bonding with DAL. Furthermore, for the four DBU-CPL-_x_ (the order for DAL solubility: DBU-CPL-2:1 > DBU-CPL-1:1 > DBU-CPL-1:2 ≈ DBU-CPL-1:3), no obvious correlations were observed between the DAL solubility and the Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters (i.e., α, β, π*, and even α-β, Table S10). For example, wood can be degraded by an acid and alkali solution in the pulping and papermaking process, rather than an acid solution or alkali solution, while cellulose or chitosan only linearly related to the β or β–α parameter. 46,47 The relationship between the lignin solubility and the values of solvatochromic parameters significantly varied from the type of lignin when the used EMLs possessed a specific HBD. As shown in Tables S4–S7 and S9, if all of the achieved EMLs were compared together, the correlation between lignin solubility and the values of solvatochromic parameters was much worse, indicating that the nature of the used EMLs may be the key parameter to affect lignin

Therefore, it could be concluded that the nature of the synthesized EMLs and the types of lignin were crucial for the relationship between lignin solubility and the solvatochromic parameters. When the ability of EMLs to dissolve lignin was estimated, this point must be paid more attention, and it would be no reason if only the solvatochromic parameters were compared.

## CONCLUSIONS In conclusion, 17 kinds of DBU-based EMLs were designed using six HBDs (i.e., CPL, BZA, PCA, PEG, LA, and NMTU) with the goal to dissolve lignin efficiently. It was found that the solubility significantly depended on the nature of the EMLs and the types of lignin. DAL could be dissolved in all the obtained DBU-based EMLs except for DBU-PEG-2:1, and most of the EMLs could dissolve EHL. However, OL was more difficult to be dissolved than DAL and EHL. Only DBU-LA-x (except for DBU-LA-1:1 with very low solubility) could dissolve OL at all examined temperatures, and higher temperatures (70 and 90 °C) were needed for other types of EMLs to dissolve OL. Meanwhile, DBU-LA-x was the only type of EMLs to dissolve SL for all examined temperatures. The systematic study revealed that the nature of the synthesized EMLs and the types of lignin significantly affected the relationship between lignin solubility and the solvatochro- mic parameters. Additionally, the DBU-based EMLs using LA and PEG as the HBDs showed better performance than those with amides (BZA, PCA, and CPL) and NMTU as the HBDs in most cases. We believe that the DBU-based EMLs have great potential to be utilized as efficient task-specific solvents for lignin dissolution, and more EMLs could be hopefully designed for efficient dissolution of lignin, which are ongoing in our group.

Preparation and Characterization of EMLs. In a typical route, DBU and the suitable HBDs (i.e., CPL, BZA, PCA, PEG, LA, and NMTU) were mixed at the molar ratio of 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, or 2:1. Then, the corresponding mixture was heated on a magnetic stirrer with a heating temperature of 25 to 60 °C (Please see Table S1) until a homogeneous liquid was generated. The examination of the viscosity of the synthesized EMLs was conducted on an Anton Paar AMVn viscosity meter using a falling ball technique. Double distilled water was used to calibrate the viscosity meter, and the repeatability uncertainty was controlled at 0.01. Meanwhile, the density of the prepared EMLs was measured using an Anton Paar DMA 5000 M density meter with the accuracy of ±5 × 10⁻⁶ g cm⁻³. The temperatures for the detection of viscosity and density were 25, 35, 45, and 55 °C.

Overlaid on this lignin structure are the words "Dissolution of Various Lignin" and a list of lignin types: "DAL, EHL, SL, OL".::> ## INTRODUCTION As the only renewable natural aromatic biopolymer, lignin could be utilized to produce various aromatic chemicals and functional materials, 1-5 which has received continuously increasing attention. Generally, an adequate solvent is necessary in most of the processes for lignin utilization. However, lignin was difficult to be dissolved in most common solvents owing to its complicated cross-linked three-dimensional structure. 6,7 Therefore, development of functional solvents to dissolve lignin is of great significance for lignin utilization, and much effort has been devoted on this important topic. To date, several solvent systems have been developed for lignin dissolution, but some specific drawbacks existed in the corresponding systems. For example, the mixture of water and some organic solvents (e.g., polysorbate, 8 y-valerolactone, 9,10 and ethanol11,12) could be employed to dissolve lignin, but the high volatility of organic solvents was the main drawback of these systems. As the alternatives of organic solvent-based systems, ionic liquid (IL)-based systems have been successfully applied in lignin dissolution. 13-17 In spite of the good solubility of lignin, IL-based systems were limited by the high cost, not so good stability, and the use of toxic reagents and/or organic solvents in their synthetic routes. 18,19 Additionally, liquid ammonia had the ability to dissolve lignin, 20 but high pressure and too low temperature hampered its large-scale application. In another aspect, it is well-known that the resources and preparation methods significantly affected the structures and properties of lignin 21-23 and thus influenced the solubility of different lignin in one specific solvent. Based on the above discussion, it is a highly attractive issue to design functional solvents with the purpose of efficiently and applicably dissolving different types of lignin. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted tremendous attention as a class of green functional solvents applied in diverse areas. 24-28 Recently, several DESs has been successfully used in the dissolution of lignin. 29-31 However, the current developed DESs were generally based on quaternary ammonium salts, and their high viscosity limited their large- scale and practical applications for lignin dissolution due to the mass transfer between lignin and DESs. 32,33 Recently, eutectic molecular liquids (EMLs), an emerging type of solvents, have been proposed. 34,35 EMLs can be generated from two or more molecular compounds via various noncovalent interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonding, σ-hole bonding, π-hole bonding, κ-hole bonding, and μ-hole bonding).34 Compared with ionic DESs, EMLs could be formed from low-cost materials with lower viscosity. Meanwhile, the components in EMLs could be easily recovered and regenerated by evaporation, a significant merit over the general ionic DESs.36 Additionally, similar with ionic DESs, the properties of EMLs could be easily tuned by changing the components. These advantages make EMLs an attractive type of solvents for lignin dissolution, and novel solvents based on EMLs could be potentially designed to dissolve lignin efficiently. When the ability of EMLs to dissolve lignin was estimated, this point must be paid more attention, and it would be no reason if only the solvatochromic parameters were compared. ## CONCLUSIONS In conclusion, 17 kinds of DBU-based EMLs were designed using six HBDs (i.e., CPL, BZA, PCA, PEG, LA, and NMTU) with the goal to dissolve lignin efficiently. It was found that the solubility significantly depended on the nature of the EMLs and the types of lignin. DAL could be dissolved in all the obtained DBU-based EMLs except for DBU-PEG-2:1, and most of the EMLs could dissolve EHL. However, OL was more difficult to be dissolved than DAL and EHL. Only DBU-LA-x (except for DBU-LA-1:1 with very low solubility) could dissolve OL at all examined temperatures, and higher temperatures (70 and 90 °C) were needed for other types of EMLs to dissolve OL. Meanwhile, DBU-LA-x was the only type of EMLs to dissolve SL for all examined temperatures. The systematic study revealed that the nature of the synthesized EMLs and the types of lignin significantly affected the relationship between lignin solubility and the solvatochro- mic parameters. Additionally, the DBU-based EMLs using LA and PEG as the HBDs showed better performance than those with amides (BZA, PCA, and CPL) and NMTU as the HBDs in most cases. We believe that the DBU-based EMLs have great potential to be utilized as efficient task-specific solvents for lignin dissolution, and more EMLs could be hopefully designed for efficient dissolution of lignin, which are ongoing in our group. ## EXPERIMENTAL SECTION **Materials.** Benzamide (BZA) and 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]-undec-7-ene (DBU) were obtained from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd. Generally, an adequate solvent is necessary in most of the processes for lignin utilization. However, lignin was difficult to be dissolved in most common solvents owing to its complicated cross-linked three-dimensional structure. 6,7 Therefore, development of functional solvents to dissolve lignin is of great significance for lignin utilization, and much effort has been devoted on this important topic. To date, several solvent systems have been developed for lignin dissolution, but some specific drawbacks existed in the corresponding systems. For example, the mixture of water and some organic solvents (e.g., polysorbate, 8 y-valerolactone, 9,10 and ethanol11,12) could be employed to dissolve lignin, but the high volatility of organic solvents was the main drawback of these systems. As the alternatives of organic solvent-based systems, ionic liquid (IL)-based systems have been successfully applied in lignin dissolution. 13-17 In spite of the good solubility of lignin, IL-based systems were limited by the high cost, not so good stability, and the use of toxic reagents and/or organic solvents in their synthetic routes. 18,19 Additionally, liquid ammonia had the ability to dissolve lignin, 20 but high pressure and too low temperature hampered its large-scale application. In another aspect, it is well-known that the resources and preparation methods significantly affected the structures and properties of lignin 21-23 and thus influenced the solubility of different lignin in one specific solvent. Based on the above discussion, it is a highly attractive issue to design functional solvents with the purpose of efficiently and applicably dissolving different types of lignin. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have attracted tremendous attention as a class of green functional solvents applied in diverse areas. 24-28 Recently, several DESs has been successfully used in the dissolution of lignin. 29-31 However, the current developed DESs were generally based on quaternary ammonium salts, and their high viscosity limited their large- scale and practical applications for lignin dissolution due to the mass transfer between lignin and DESs. 32,33 Recently, eutectic molecular liquids (EMLs), an emerging type of solvents, have been proposed. 34,35 EMLs can be generated from two or more molecular compounds via various noncovalent interactions (e.g., hydrogen bonding, σ-hole bonding, π-hole bonding, κ-hole bonding, and μ-hole bonding).34 Compared with ionic DESs, EMLs could be formed from low-cost materials with lower viscosity. Meanwhile, the components in EMLs could be easily recovered and regenerated by evaporation, a significant merit over the general ionic DESs.36 Additionally, similar with ionic DESs, the properties of EMLs could be easily tuned by changing the components. These advantages make EMLs an attractive type of solvents for lignin dissolution, and novel solvents based on EMLs could be potentially designed to dissolve lignin efficiently. For example, wood can be degraded by an acid and alkali solution in the pulping and papermaking process, rather than an acid solution or alkali solution, while cellulose or chitosan only linearly related to the β or β–α parameter. 46,47 The relationship between the lignin solubility and the values of solvatochromic parameters significantly varied from the type of lignin when the used EMLs possessed a specific HBD. When the ability of EMLs to dissolve lignin was estimated, this point must be paid more attention, and it would be no reason if only the solvatochromic parameters were compared. ## CONCLUSIONS In conclusion, 17 kinds of DBU-based EMLs were designed using six HBDs (i.e., CPL, BZA, PCA, PEG, LA, and NMTU) with the goal to dissolve lignin efficiently. It was found that the solubility significantly depended on the nature of the EMLs and the types of lignin. DAL could be dissolved in all the obtained DBU-based EMLs except for DBU-PEG-2:1, and most of the EMLs could dissolve EHL. However, OL was more difficult to be dissolved than DAL and EHL. Only DBU-LA-x (except for DBU-LA-1:1 with very low solubility) could dissolve OL at all examined temperatures, and higher temperatures (70 and 90 °C) were needed for other types of EMLs to dissolve OL. Meanwhile, DBU-LA-x was the only type of EMLs to dissolve SL for all examined temperatures. The systematic study revealed that the nature of the synthesized EMLs and the types of lignin significantly affected the relationship between lignin solubility and the solvatochro- mic parameters. Additionally, the DBU-based EMLs using LA and PEG as the HBDs showed better performance than those with amides (BZA, PCA, and CPL) and NMTU as the HBDs in most cases. We believe that the DBU-based EMLs have great potential to be utilized as efficient task-specific solvents for lignin dissolution, and more EMLs could be hopefully designed for efficient dissolution of lignin, which are ongoing in our group. ## EXPERIMENTAL SECTION **Materials.** Benzamide (BZA) and 1,8-diazabicyclo[5.4.0]-undec-7-ene (DBU) were obtained from Beijing Innochem Technology Co., Ltd. Preparation and Characterization of EMLs. In a typical route, DBU and the suitable HBDs (i.e., CPL, BZA, PCA, PEG, LA, and NMTU) were mixed at the molar ratio of 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, or 2:1. Then, the corresponding mixture was heated on a magnetic stirrer with a heating temperature of 25 to 60 °C (Please see Table S1) until a homogeneous liquid was generated. At last, the achieved liquids were heated at 60 °C for 24 h under vacuum to remove the contained water, and the desired EMLs were finally obtained. The examination of the viscosity of the synthesized EMLs was conducted on an Anton Paar AMVn viscosity meter using a falling ball technique. Double distilled water was used to calibrate the viscosity meter, and the repeatability uncertainty was controlled at 0.01. Meanwhile, the density of the prepared EMLs was measured using an Anton Paar DMA 5000 M density meter with the accuracy of ±5 × 10⁻⁶ g cm⁻³. The temperatures for the detection of viscosity and density were 25, 35, 45, and 55 °C. Solubility of Lignin.
